subject: Accounting
title: The Matching Principle
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Matching Principle usable.

hook.text: A company spends $50,000 on ads in March. Sales spike in April. Which month gets the cost?

buildup.text: The matching principle says expenses go in the same period as the revenue they help create.

discovery.text: This stops companies from front-loading or delaying expenses to manipulate profits.

twist.text: Depreciation exists because of this rule—spread a machine's cost across its useful life.

climax.text: Without matching, a company could look wildly profitable one quarter and broke the next.

punchline.text: Match the expense to the revenue it helped create.

quiz.question: What does the matching principle require?
options: Record expenses when related revenue is earned
Delay expenses until cash is paid

details.summary: The matching principle requires that expenses be recognized in the same period as the revenue they help generate. Selling product in December means December bears the cost of goods sold, even if the supplier was paid in November.
details.whyItMatters: Without matching, profit calculation would be meaningless—costs could appear in different periods than the revenue they generated, making it impossible to assess actual performance.
takeaways: Expenses are matched to the revenue they directly help produce in the same accounting period
Depreciation spreads asset costs over the periods that benefit from the asset's use
Matching drives most adjusting entries at period-end, including accrued expenses and prepaid allocations

faq.question: How does the matching principle work in practice?
faq.answer: If a company pays $12,000 in January for a full year of insurance, the matching principle allocates $1,000 per month rather than recording the entire cost in January. Each month bears only its fair share of the expense, matching the cost to the period that benefits.

faq.question: What happens when costs can't be matched to specific revenue?
faq.answer: Costs that can't be directly traced to revenue—like executive salaries, rent, and utilities—are recorded as period expenses in the period incurred. Only costs with a direct cause-and-effect relationship to revenue (like cost of goods sold) are matched to specific revenue.
